pos: n. (the mother house of the Premonstratensian order, founded by Norbert of Xanten in 1120 in Picardy)
etymology: Latin Praemonstratum, the place shown beforehand; French pré montré, the meadow pointed out.
biblical_def: Prémontré lies in a wooded valley of the Aisne in Picardy, and the name was explained from the first as the place shown beforehand, the meadow pointed out to Norbert for his foundation. He settled there in 1120 with a handful of followers, adopted the Rule of Augustine, and within a generation the order had houses from Spain to Livonia. The abbey was rebuilt in the eighteenth century on a grand scale, dissolved at the Revolution, and the buildings have been a psychiatric hospital since 1867. This dictionary records Prémontré for its name, because the claim buried in it is one Scripture handles with great care. God does show men places and tell men things, “I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision” (Num 12:6), and a people without that word goes to pieces, “Where there is no vision, the people perish” (Pro 29:18). But the way of speaking has changed and the change is announced, “God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets” (Heb 1:1). What remains is a more certain word than any private showing, “We have also a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vision as something apparently seen otherwise than by ordinary sight; revelation as the disclosure of truth by God; a meadow as low grass land; prophecy as a foretelling; and a founder as one who establishes.
webster_full: VISION, n. The act of seeing external objects; sight; also, something imaginary; a revelation made to a prophet in sleep or trance.
REVELATION, n. The act of disclosing or discovering to others what was before unknown; appropriately, the disclosure or communication of truth to men by God himself.
MEADOW, n. A tract of low land, appropriated to the production of grass for hay; grass land annually mown.
PROPHECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come; in Scripture, a book of prophecies.
FOUNDER, n. One that founds, establishes and erects; one from whom any thing originates.
scriptures: Num 12:6
And he said, Hear now my words: If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream.
Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.
Heb 1:1
God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
corruption_summary: Mother house of the Premonstratensians, 1120: the place said to have been shown beforehand, and a name that raises the question of how God speaks now.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture does not deny God's speaking; it dates it and ranks it. Visions were a real mode, “If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision” (Num 12:6), and a people left without a word unravel, “Where there is no vision, the people perish” (Pro 29:18).

The live error in our own time is the inflation of the word vision into a term for ambition or a planning document, and alongside it the claim that a place or a project was divinely indicated. Hebrews marks a change of mode so decisively that everything after it is measured by the Son rather than by a showing, “spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets” (Heb 1:1). Peter, who had actually seen the transfiguration, nevertheless points his readers away from his own experience to the written word, “whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place” (2Pe 1:19). A meadow may be a good site without being a message.

pos: n. (the Rhineland Premonstratensian abbey of 1130, with its great apse fresco of Christ in majesty)
etymology: German Knecht, a servant or bondman, and Steden, places or steads; the servants' steads.
biblical_def: Knechtsteden near Dormagen in the Rhineland was founded in 1130 by Hugo of Sponheim as a Premonstratensian house. Its basilica, consecrated in 1181, is a complete Rhenish Romanesque church with apses at both ends, and the western apse carries a fresco of Christ in majesty between Peter and Paul, painted about 1162, which is among the best preserved Romanesque wall paintings in Germany. The abbey was secularised in 1802 and burnt in 1869; since 1895 it has been a mission house of the Spiritans. This dictionary records Knechtsteden for its name, which is simply the German for servants, and which is the title Scripture gives to the greatest of its figures. The Servant is the chosen of God, “Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth” (Isa 42:1). The Son takes the form by choice, “took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men” (Phi 2:7), and gives the reason, “the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister” (Mat 20:28). And the servant who has done everything required still has no claim, “We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do” (Luk 17:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a servant as one who attends another; to minister as to serve or supply; a bondman as a man slave; duty as that which a person is bound to perform; and humility as lowliness of mind.
webster_full: SERVANT, n. A person, male or female, that attends another for the purpose of performing menial offices for him, or who is employed by another for such offices.
MINISTER, v.t. To give; to afford; to supply; to serve in any office or duty; to attend and serve.
BONDMAN, n. A man slave, or one bound to service without wages; a villain or tenant in villenage.
DUTY, n. That which a person owes to another; that which a person is bound by any natural, moral or legal obligation to pay, do or perform.
HUMILITY, n. In ethics, freedom from pride and arrogance; lowliness of mind; a modest estimate of one's own worth.
scriptures: Isa 42:1
Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles.
Phi 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.
So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.
corruption_summary: Rhineland Premonstratensian abbey of 1130, the servants' steads: a Romanesque basilica whose apse shows the Servant in majesty.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the fresco and the name belong together. A church named for servants and painted with Christ in glory is saying what Philippians says in a sentence: the one in majesty is the one who took the servant's form, “took upon him the form of a servant” (Phi 2:7), and Isaiah had already given him the title with God's own delight attached, “mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth” (Isa 42:1).

The live corruption is servant language used as a credential. A great deal of modern religious speech describes leadership as service while keeping every advantage of rank. The Lord's own statement is not a style of leading but an account of why he came and what it cost, “and to give his life a ransom for many” (Mat 20:28). And the parable removes the last foothold for self-congratulation from anyone who has merely done his job, “We are unprofitable servants” (Luk 17:10).

pos: n. (the Wetterau Premonstratensian abbey of 1123, endowed by Gottfried of Cappenberg)
etymology: From a Germanic personal name with Stadt, a place or settlement.
biblical_def: Ilbenstadt in the Wetterau north of Frankfurt was founded in 1123 and given to Norbert's new order, and its Romanesque basilica of about 1159 survives nearly intact. Its endowment came from Gottfried, count of Cappenberg in Westphalia, who in 1122 handed Norbert his ancestral castle and his entire inheritance to be made into monasteries, over the furious objection of his father-in-law, and who entered the order himself and died at twenty-six. His brother Otto followed him. Ilbenstadt holds the graves of both. This dictionary records Ilbenstadt because Gottfried did what the rich young ruler would not, and the comparison is worth making carefully. The command was given to one man whose possessions held him, “go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor” (Mar 10:21), and the refusal is one of the saddest lines in the Gospels, “he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions” (Mat 19:22). Christ says plainly where a heart will be found, “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Mat 6:21), and he names the choice as a choice between masters, “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor; to renounce as to disown or reject; patrimony as an estate inherited from one's father; endowment as a permanent provision; and mammon as riches, wealth personified.
webster_full: INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; an estate which a man has by descent, as the heir to another.
RENOUNCE, v.t. To disown; to disclaim; to reject; to cast off; to forsake; as, to renounce a claim or a title.
PATRIMONY, n. A right or estate inherited from one's ancestors; particularly, from a father; a church estate or revenue.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of an institution; the fund so settled.
MAMMON, n. Riches; wealth; or the god of riches; a word used by our Saviour as the personification of worldly gain.
scriptures: Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me.
But when the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions.
Mat 6:21
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
Mat 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
corruption_summary: Wetterau abbey of 1123, endowed by a count who gave Norbert his castle and his whole inheritance and died a canon at twenty-six.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the diagnostic. The command to sell was given to a particular man because his possessions had him, and Christ's general rule explains why he could put it that way, “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Mat 6:21). Gottfried of Cappenberg handed over castles his family had held for generations, and his relatives reacted exactly as one would expect.

The caution is against reading this as a universal rule or a merit. Scripture does not command every believer to divest, and it never treats poverty as purchase. What it does is force a choice of master, in terms that allow no arrangement, “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24). The rich young man heard the same words and left, and the text gives his reason without comment, “for he had great possessions” (Mat 19:22). The question is not how much a man has but which way he walks when told to let go.

pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey on the Lahn, founded 1139 when the last count of Arnstein gave up his castle)
etymology: German Aar, an eagle, and Stein, a stone; the eagle's rock.
biblical_def: Arnstein stands on a crag above the Lahn in the Taunus. In 1139 Count Ludwig III of Arnstein, the last of his line, gave his castle to the Premonstratensians, converted it into an abbey, and entered it himself as a lay brother, living in a cell by the gate until his death in 1185; his wife Guda entered an enclosure of her own. The church, consecrated in 1208, has an unusual plan with apses at both ends, and the abbey survived until 1803. This dictionary records Arnstein for the decision of a man with no heir, because Scripture takes the question of what becomes of an estate seriously rather than sentimentally. The law made careful provision when there was no son, “then ye shall cause his inheritance to pass unto his daughter” (Num 27:8). A good man leaves something behind on purpose, “A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children” (Pro 13:22). The portion a believer actually holds is described with contentment rather than calculation, “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage” (Psa 16:6), and the inheritance that cannot be spent is held elsewhere, “To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away” (1Pe 1:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an heir as one who succeeds to an estate; an inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor; a castle as a fortified house; to bequeath as to give by will; and a lineage as a race or family descending from a progenitor.
webster_full: HEIR, n. The man who succeeds, or is to succeed another in the possession of lands, tenements and hereditaments, by descent.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; an estate which a man has by descent.
CASTLE, n. A house fortified for defense against an enemy; a fortress; the house of a prince or nobleman.
BEQUEATH, v.t. To give or leave by will; to devise some species of property by testament; as, to bequeath an estate to a son.
LINEAGE, n. Race; progeny; descendants in a line from a common progenitor.
scriptures: Num 27:8
And thou shalt speak unto the children of Israel, saying, If a man die, and have no son, then ye shall cause his inheritance to pass unto his daughter.
A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.
Psa 16:6
The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.
To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you,
corruption_summary: Premonstratensian abbey on the Lahn, 1139: the last count of his line turned his castle into it and lived there as a lay brother for forty-six years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an estate is a trust with a destination, and Scripture legislates about it in detail rather than waving it away. When a man died without a son the inheritance was not simply lost, “then ye shall cause his inheritance to pass unto his daughter” (Num 27:8), and leaving something to the generation after next is set down as the mark of a good man, “A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children” (Pro 13:22).

The second thing is Ludwig's own position. He had no heir, and instead of letting his lands be fought over he converted them to a use that outlasted his family by six centuries, and then took the lowest place in the house he had founded. The psalm describes that settledness exactly, “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places” (Psa 16:6), and Peter names the only portion that is finally secure, “reserved in heaven for you” (1Pe 1:4). A man who has that one can be generous with the other.

pos: n. (the Eifel Premonstratensian abbey, whose Renaissance cloister glass is now scattered across England)
etymology: German Stein, a stone, and Feld, a field; the stony field.
biblical_def: Steinfeld in the Eifel became Premonstratensian in 1121 and was for centuries the head of a circary of houses. Its Romanesque basilica survives, and so does the memory of Hermann Joseph, a thirteenth-century canon of the house known for his devotional writing. Its cloister once held a celebrated series of stained glass windows made between 1526 and 1557; after the abbey was dissolved in 1802 the glass was sold, and most of it is now in the Victoria and Albert Museum and in English parish churches, with panels scattered as far as Ashridge and Shrewsbury. This dictionary records Steinfeld for its name, the stony field, which is an exact phrase from one of the Lord's plainest parables. Seed falls on stony ground and springs quickly, “Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth” (Mat 13:5), and withers for the same reason it rose, “because they had no root, they withered away” (Mat 13:6). The Lord interprets it himself as a man who receives the word with joy and fails under pressure, “when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended” (Mat 13:21). God's own answer to a stony field is to replace the stone, “I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh” (Eze 36:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stony as full of stones or hard like stone; a field as land enclosed for tillage; a root as the part of a plant which enters the earth; tribulation as severe affliction; and to wither as to fade or dry up.
webster_full: STONY, adj. Made of stone; abounding with stones; full of stones; also, hard; cruel; unrelenting; as a stony heart.
FIELD, n. A piece of land enclosed for tillage or pasture; any part of the open country not covered with wood.
ROOT, n. That part of a plant which enters and fixes itself in the earth, and serves to support the plant and supply it with nourishment.
TRIBULATION, n. Severe affliction; distresses of life; vexations; in Scripture, troubles and distresses which proceed from persecution.
WITHER, v.i. To fade; to lose its native freshness; to become sapless; to dry.
scriptures: Mat 13:5
Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth:
Mat 13:6
And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.
Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
corruption_summary: Eifel Premonstratensian abbey, the stony field: its Renaissance cloister glass was sold in 1802 and is now scattered through English museums and churches.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Lord's own diagnosis, which is uncomfortable because the stony ground looks like the best ground at first. The seed comes up fastest there, “where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up” (Mat 13:5), and the very thinness that makes for speed makes for collapse, “and because they had no root, they withered away” (Mat 13:6). An enthusiastic response is not yet evidence of anything.

The second thing is that the remedy is not more enthusiasm. Christ names the point of failure precisely as pressure from outside, “when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended” (Mat 13:21), and Ezekiel supplies the only cure, which is a transplant rather than an effort, “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you” (Eze 36:26). A field full of stone can be cleared, and only God clears this one.

pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey of 1136 at Duisburg, refounded in 1959 inside a steel city)
etymology: From Low German ham, an enclosed meadow, and born, a spring.
biblical_def: Hamborn on the lower Rhine was given to the Premonstratensians in 1136 and served the surrounding countryside for six centuries until its dissolution in 1806. In the nineteenth century the countryside vanished: the Thyssen works were built beside it, the population went from a few hundred to more than a hundred thousand in forty years, and the old abbey church found itself the parish church of a steel town. Canons returned in 1959, and the abbey now runs a hospital and parishes among the furnaces. This dictionary records Hamborn because an abbey that woke up inside an industrial city is a picture of a question the church keeps having to answer. Scripture does not tell exiles to withdraw from the city they are in; it tells them to work for it, “seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it” (Jer 29:7). The reason given is self-interested and unembarrassed, “for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer 29:7). Peacemaking is a blessing attached to a name, “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God” (Mat 5:9), and the obligation is as wide as it can be made, “as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a city as a large town incorporated; a parish as the precinct committed to one minister; industry as habitual diligence in business; peace as freedom from war or disturbance; and a neighbour as one who lives near another.
webster_full: CITY, n. In a general sense, a large town; a large number of houses and inhabitants, established in one place; a corporate town.
PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.
INDUSTRY, n. Habitual diligence in any employment, either bodily or mental; steady attention to business; assiduity.
PEACE, n. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from disturbance or agitation; freedom from war.
NEIGHBOR, n. One who lives near another; in Scripture, any one whom we may benefit; a fellow being.
scriptures: Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Mat 5:9
Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.
corruption_summary: Premonstratensian abbey of 1136 at Duisburg: a country house that woke to find a steel city around it, and went to work in it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Jeremiah's instruction to people who had every reason to disengage. They were captives in a pagan city, and the word to them was to build, plant, marry and pray for the place, “seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives” (Jer 29:7), with a plain reason attached, “for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer 29:7).

The live temptation is the opposite of the monastic one and just as old: a congregation that treats the city around it as scenery. The blessing Christ pronounces is on the people who actually make peace rather than merely enjoy it, “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Mat 5:9), and Paul sets the obligation about as wide as language allows while being honest about its limits, “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18). Paul also leaves a saying of the Lord not recorded in the Gospels, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Act 20:35), which is a reasonable charter for an abbey running a hospital.

usage: “seek the peace of the city” (Jer 29:7) — said to exiles, not to citizens.
“as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18) — wide, and honest about its limit.
“It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Act 20:35) — a saying of the Lord kept only by Paul.

pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey near Neuwied, founded 1135, preserved through centuries of farm use)
etymology: From a Germanic personal name Rumold with Dorf, a village.
biblical_def: Rommersdorf near Neuwied on the middle Rhine was founded about 1117 as a house of Augustinian canons and became Premonstratensian in 1135. It kept a modest but complete set of buildings: church, cloister, chapter house, refectory, gatehouse and a vaulted abbot's hall. Dissolved in 1803, it passed into private hands and was worked as a farm for a century and a half, which is precisely why so much survives. A farmer who needs a barn keeps the roof on; a speculator who needs stone does not. It is now restored and used for concerts. This dictionary records Rommersdorf for that accidental preservation, which illustrates a principle Scripture states directly about small faithfulness. The man who is dependable in a little is dependable in much, “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luk 16:10). The commendation in the parable is for the keeping rather than the scale, “thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things” (Mat 25:21). Stewards are judged by one quality, “it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2), and the day of small things is explicitly not despised, “who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a steward as one who manages for another; faithful as firm in adherence to duty; to preserve as to keep from injury; a tenant as one who holds lands of another; and husbandry as the business of a farmer.
webster_full: STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants, and receive and pay money.
FAITHFUL, adj. Firm in adherence to the truth and to the duties of religion; true to the marriage covenant; constant in the performance of duties.
PRESERVE, v.t. To keep or save from injury or destruction; to defend from evil; to uphold; to save from decay.
TENANT, n. One who holds or possesses lands or tenements by any kind of right, whether in fee simple, in common, or for life.
HUSBANDRY, n. The business of a farmer, comprehending agriculture or tillage of the ground, the raising and managing of cattle.
scriptures: He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
Zec 4:10

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
corruption_summary: Premonstratensian abbey near Neuwied, 1135: it survived not by fame but because a farmer kept the roof on for a hundred and fifty years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faithfulness is tested at a scale nobody is watching. Rommersdorf has no great glass, no famous abbot and no celebrated library; it has a complete medieval cloister because somebody kept using it and kept it dry. Christ states the rule in both directions, “and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much” (Luk 16:10), and the master in the parable commends the quantity of nothing, only the fidelity, “Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Mat 25:21).

The second thing is what a steward is actually measured by. Paul reduces the whole job description to one requirement, “it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2), and Zechariah forbids the contempt that makes men neglect what is merely small, “For who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10). Most of what survives from any century survives this way, through people doing unremarkable maintenance for reasons nobody recorded.

pos: n. (the Saarland Premonstratensian abbey of 1135, whose site became a glassworks)
etymology: From Old High German, the dwelling at the ford; wad, a ford, and gassen, lanes.
biblical_def: Wadgassen on the Saar was founded in 1135 by Count Frederick of Saarbrücken and given to the Premonstratensians, and it held lands on both banks of a river that would become one of Europe's most contested borders. It was destroyed by French troops in 1793 and finally dissolved in 1795. In 1843 Villeroy & Boch bought the site and built a glassworks on it, which ran until 1995; the abbey's library, remarkably, survived and is now a museum of printing. This dictionary records Wadgassen for the glass, because Scripture uses glass for one purpose above all others, and it is not decoration. We see indirectly now, “For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face” (1Co 13:12), and the knowing is correspondingly partial, “now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known” (1Co 13:12). The same figure is used of a man who forgets what he looked like, “he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass” (Jam 1:23), and the glass that does change a man is the one that shows him Christ, “But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image” (2Co 3:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines glass as a hard brittle transparent substance; a mirror as a looking glass; transparent as admitting light so objects can be seen through; to reflect as to throw back rays; and darkly as obscurely.
webster_full: GLASS, n. A hard, brittle, transparent, factitious substance, formed by fusing sand with fixed alkalies; also, a looking glass; a mirror.
MIRROR, n. A looking glass; any glass or polished substance that forms images by the reflection of rays of light.
TRANSPARENT, adj. Having the property of transmitting rays of light, so that bodies can be distinctly seen through; pervious to light.
REFLECT, v.t. To throw back; as, a mirror reflects the rays of light; to cast back the image of.
DARKLY, adv. Obscurely; dimly; blindly; uncertainly; with imperfect light, clearness or knowledge.
scriptures: For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
Jam 1:23
For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass:
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
Col 2:3
In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
corruption_summary: Saarland Premonstratensian abbey of 1135: destroyed in the Revolution, rebuilt as a glassworks, and its library survives as a museum of printing.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's honesty about how much we currently see. The mirrors of the ancient world were polished metal and gave a dim, warped image, which is exactly the force of the figure, “For now we see through a glass, darkly” (1Co 13:12). He applies it to knowledge without flinching, “now I know in part” (1Co 13:12), which is a useful corrective to anyone certain he has the whole picture.

The second use of the figure is moral. James describes a man who looks in a glass and walks away having forgotten his own face, which is his picture of hearing without doing, “he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass” (Jam 1:23). Against that, Paul describes a looking that actually transforms the looker, “are changed into the same image from glory to glory” (2Co 3:18). The treasures a man is actually looking for are located in one place, “In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col 2:3).

“beholding his natural face in a glass” (Jam 1:23) — hearing without doing.

pos: n. (the Upper Swabian Premonstratensian abbey of 1183, famous for its rococo library hall)
etymology: From the river Schussen and German Ried, a reed marsh.
biblical_def: Schussenried in Upper Swabia was founded in 1183 by two brothers of the local nobility and given to the Premonstratensians. It prospered quietly for six hundred years and then, in the eighteenth century, rebuilt itself in rococo; its library hall, finished in 1766 with a ceiling fresco by Franz Georg Hermann and a gallery of carved figures, is among the most extravagant rooms in Germany. The abbey was dissolved in 1803, and its buildings served as a psychiatric hospital for most of the twentieth century. This dictionary records Schussenried for its library, and for the double word Scripture gives about books. The accumulation of them has a limit, and the Preacher says so in a sentence every scholar should keep on his desk, “of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh” (Ecc 12:12). Yet wisdom is to be dug for like silver, “If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures” (Pro 2:4), and it is ranked above everything a man might acquire instead, “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom” (Pro 4:7), because the whole hoard is finally in one person, “In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col 2:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a library as a collection of books; study as application of mind to books; wisdom as the right use of knowledge; learning as acquired knowledge; and weariness as the state of being tired.
webster_full: LIBRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution or a company.
STUDY, n. Application of mind to books, to arts or science, or to any subject, for the purpose of learning what is not before known.
WISDOM, n. The right use or exercise of knowledge; the choice of laudable ends, and of the best means to accomplish them.
LEARNING, n. The knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study; acquired knowledge or ideas in any branch of science or literature.
WEARINESS, n. The state of being weary or tired; lassitude; fatigue from labor or exertion.
scriptures: And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
Pro 2:4
If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures;
Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
Col 2:3
In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
corruption_summary: Upper Swabian Premonstratensian abbey of 1183: its rococo library hall is among the most extravagant rooms in Germany.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the balance Scripture actually holds. It does not despise books, and it does set a ceiling on them, “of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh” (Ecc 12:12). The weariness is named as real rather than as a failure of character. A gilded library hall is a splendid thing and will not make anybody wise.

What Scripture presses instead is effort of a different kind, searching for wisdom the way men dig for silver, “and searchest for her as for hid treasures” (Pro 2:4), with the priority settled before the search begins, “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding” (Pro 4:7). The location of the hoard is finally a person rather than a collection, “In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col 2:3), which is a sobering sentence to read under a painted ceiling.

pos: n. (the Swabian Premonstratensian abbey of 1126, refounded in 1982)
etymology: German Roggen, rye, and Burg, a stronghold; the rye castle.
biblical_def: Roggenburg in Bavarian Swabia was founded in 1126 by the brothers Berthold and Siegfried of Biberegg and given to the Premonstratensians. Its church was rebuilt between 1752 and 1758 to a design of Simpert Krämer and is one of the great rococo interiors of the region, with an organ to match. Dissolved in 1802, Roggenburg was resettled by Norbertines in 1982 and now runs a school and an education centre. This dictionary records Roggenburg for the grain in its name, and for the one thing Scripture says about a seed that most farming proverbs do not. Grain must die before it multiplies, “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit” (Joh 12:24). The Lord says it of himself, and Paul extends the figure to the resurrection of the body. Bread made from that grain is given a name, “I am the bread of life” (Joh 6:35), and man is told not to live by bread alone, “man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD” (Deu 8:3). The famine to dread is not of grain, “not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines corn as grain in general; wheat as a plant of the genus Triticum; bread as food made of flour; a harvest as the season of reaping; and famine as a scarcity of food.
webster_full: CORN, n. A single seed of certain plants, as wheat, rye, barley and maize; in America, the seeds of maize; in Great Britain, grain in general.
WHEAT, n. A plant of the genus Triticum, and its seed, of which the finest bread is made.
BREAD, n. Food made of flour or meal; also, food in general; support of life.
HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering in corn or other crops; the ripe corn or grain collected.
FAMINE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient for the inhabitants of a country or besieged place.
scriptures: Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
Joh 6:35
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Deu 8:3

And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live.
Amo 8:11
Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:
corruption_summary: Swabian Premonstratensian abbey of 1126, the rye castle: dissolved in 1802, resettled by Norbertines in 1982, and running a school again.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one that farming alone would never teach. A seed that is kept is wasted, and only a seed that is buried multiplies, “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone” (Joh 12:24). The Lord says this of his own death and then applies it to his followers, which is why the sentence is more than agricultural observation.

The second thing is the order of bread and word. Christ takes the name of the loaf for himself, “I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger” (Joh 6:35), and the wilderness lesson Moses draws is that bread was never the sustaining thing, “man doth not live by bread only” (Deu 8:3). Amos names the famine actually worth fearing, and it is a famine a prosperous country can have without noticing, “but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11). An abbey named for rye, teaching school again after a hundred and eighty years, is in the right business.
